title: The road to self-driving laboratories in industry
key_facts: A Nature Synthesis editorial introduces an issue on self-driving laboratories for making molecules and materials, with a focus on industry.
Self-driving labs combine robotics, automation and AI to plan and run experiments; moving them from academic proof of concept to industry can be challenging.
RoboChem-Flex, a modular platform from Timothy Noël's group, costs around US$5,000, which the editorial says could make such labs more accessible.
Bartosz Grzybowski's group used a robotic platform to find a new seven-component reaction based on the century-old Biginelli reaction.
A comment by Linjiang Chen and colleagues argues industrial self-driving labs need an "autonomy safety harness" governing how AI plans become experiments.
Contributors include researchers from AbbVie, AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Eli Lilly, Genentech, NVIDIA, Takeda and others.
quote_evidence: Self-driving laboratories, which combine robotics, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) to autonomously plan and run experiments, are being used to accelerate research.
Moving this technology from academic proof of concept to industrial practice, however, can be challenging.
why_it_matters_hint: An industry-focused overview of how automated chemistry labs are spreading and what holds them back.
notes: An editorial overview, not a single new finding. Publication date not shown on the page.
